newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Chirac presses ahead with reforms, euro.
newsitem.headline: France's Chirac presses ahead with reforms, euro.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac, in a vibrant defence of Europe, reaffirmed on Thursday his determination to join the single European currency despite a plunge in popularity over budget cuts and record unemployment.

In his first extended public statement since July, Chirac defended austerity policies to meet the Maastricht criteria and said the single European currency was the key to reviving the sluggish economy and give Europe the power to challenge U.S. "hegemony".

"We are not making sacrifices for the single currency. We are building a system that will give us the means of stability inside (the EU) and power outside," he said in a live prime-time television interview.
"This is why we need to achieve the Euro and this is why we will achieve it," he said.
He said he believed the EU would reach agreement, perhaps during the crucial EU summit opening on Friday in Dublin, on a "stability pact" on budgetary discipline in the future euro currency zone.

He again rejected calls for a devaluation of the franc against the German mark that could help revive the economy, saying such a move would amount to breaking the Franco-German partnership that is the key to European construction.

Chirac said he had no intention of reshuffling his cabinet. He praised the courage of fellow-Gaullist Prime Minister Alain Juppe, who was carrying out reforms undeterred by being the most unpopular French premier in modern times.
A CSA opinion poll released on Wednesday found that 54 percent of French voters want Juppe out as prime minister.
Many commentators have speculated that he will order a reshuffle sometime next year to streamline the government for elections scheduled in 1998.

Chirac endeavoured in the 90-minute interview on TF1 television to restore confidence in the government, placing the emphasis on the need to press ahead with reforms despite resistance from a country he called conservative and hampered by traditions and fear of the future.

His only announcement was that he had asked the government to further cut taxes in a fiscal reform, and that he had appointed a commission to reform the judiciary and see how to strengthen the independence of prosecutors and bolster the presumption of innocence for suspects.

Grilled at length for the first time since he came to office in 1995 about suspected political kickbacks and sleaze probes into political parties including his own, Chirac said: "Probes must be carried out to the end and punishment must be all the more exemplary as it concerns people in position of power."

Chirac had no disclosures on a bomb attack which killed four people on a Paris commuter train last week. He said police were working intensely and following up all possible leads, but it was too early to say where the probe would lead.
The attack has been blamed on Algerian Moslem rebels protesting against French aid to Algeria who were also held responsible for last year's bombings which killed eight people in France.
Chirac ruled out breaking off economic relations with Algiers, saying isolating the government of President Liamine Zeroual could lead to chaos and would be irresponsible.
Accused of going back on campaign pledges to put priority on curbing unemployment and fighting rising poverty, Chirac said he was not repudiating any of his commitments.
"All this is possible only if we first put our house in order, including our finances. We must first carry out the reforms that are necessary," he said.
